summary: This Standards Track document specifies the MPLS Network Action sub-stack, which carries network actions and ancillary data in the MPLS label stack. These can influence forwarding, carry OAM information, or perform user-defined operations. It updates RFC 9789 to refine the information that must appear in documents defining such actions.

eli5.summary: Packets carry little instruction tags in their label stack, telling routers what extra thing to do.

questions: what is an mpls network action sub-stack
subtitle: How to tuck small instructions and data for routers into the MPLS label stack itself.

tldr.problem: Some MPLS applications need packets to trigger special network actions and carry small amounts of ancillary data, but the plain label stack has no standard way to encode them.
tldr.mechanism: A Network Action Sub-Stack (NAS) starts with a label stack entry holding the special-purpose label 4, followed by entries in Formats B, C and D that carry 7-bit opcodes and their data.
tldr.outcome: It gives MNA a common encoding, rules for where to place and process the sub-stack, and updates RFC 9789 with a refined list of what any document defining a new network action must specify.

today: RFC 9994 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026 that updates RFC 9789. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Put Actions in the Label Stack
sections.content:
RFC 3032 defines how an MPLS label stack is encoded, and that stack is what defines a forwarding path. Some applications need MPLS packets to perform special network actions and to carry optional Ancillary Data (AD) that can affect the forwarding decision or trigger Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) logging. AD can also carry information for network slice purposes.

This document defines the syntax and semantics of those actions and data when they are encoded in the label stack. They live in a Network Action Sub-Stack (NAS), which is recognized by a new base Special-Purpose Label (bSPL). It follows the framework of RFC 9789.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a packet needs to carry a small note that tells routers to do an extra job. This RFC says exactly how to write that note inside the packet's label stack.

sections.title: The Sub-Stack at a Glance
sections.content:
A NAS is a set of label stack entries (LSEs) that sit inside an MPLS label stack. Several NASes may appear in one stack. Beyond the LSE of RFC 3032, three new LSE formats carry 7 bits of network action opcode plus varying amounts of opcode-specific data.

The first LSE of a sub-stack uses Format A. The second uses Format B, optionally followed by Format D entries for extra data. After that there may be Format C entries for further actions, each optionally followed by Format D entries. Format B carries up to 13 bits of AD in an LSE, Format C up to 20 bits, and Format D is used when the opcodes in B or C need more.
sections.eli5: Think of a row of cards. The first card says 'special instructions start here'. The next cards each hold one instruction and maybe a few extra details.

sections.title: The Four Label Stack Entry Formats
sections.content:
Format A is an ordinary LSE whose label value is 4, the MNA bSPL, marking the start of a sub-stack. Its S (bottom of stack) bit MUST be 0 when sent, and a packet received with label 4 and S set to 1 MUST be dropped.

Format B holds the first opcode: a 7-bit Opcode, 13 bits of data, a reserved bit, the 2-bit IHS scope, S, a 4-bit NASL (the number of Format C and D entries that follow), the 1-bit U unknown-action flag and a 3-bit NAL (the number of Format D entries attached to this opcode). Format C holds each later opcode with 16 plus 4 bits of data, S, U and NAL.

Format D carries only extra data: 22 bits plus 8 bits. Its most significant bit MUST be set, so legacy implementations do not mistake it for a special-purpose label when the data begins with zeros. A Format A and a Format B entry MUST be present whenever Format C or D entries are used.

Many length and S-bit checks apply. For example, NAL MUST NOT exceed NASL, and S may be 1 only in the last LSE of the stack; otherwise the packet MUST be dropped.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of cards. One says 'start', two hold an instruction, and one is just extra room for details. Each card has a few little checkboxes that tell you how many cards come next.

sections.title: Scope, Unknown Actions and Ordering
sections.content:
The IHS field sets the scope of every action in a NAS. 00 is Ingress to Egress (I2E): only the egress node processes it. 01 is Hop-by-Hop (HbH): all nodes along the path MUST process it. 10 is Select: only specific nodes that bring the NAS to the top of the stack act on it. 11 is reserved. A NAS carries actions of one scope only, but a stack may hold several NASes. An I2E NAS, if present, MUST come after any HbH or Select NAS.

The U bit says what a node that does not understand an action should do: 0 skips to the next action and 1 drops the packet. A node that drops should keep a local counter and may send a rate-limited notification to the operator.

Actions are processed in the order they appear, top to bottom. Flag-based actions are processed from the most significant bit to the least significant.
sections.eli5: Some notes are for every stop on the trip, some only for the last stop, and some only for certain stops. A flag also says whether a stop that does not understand a note should skip it or throw the parcel away.

sections.title: Opcodes and Ancillary Data
sections.content:
Opcode 0 is reserved: keeping the opcode non-zero ensures the first 20 bits of an LSE can never look like a bSPL (0 to 15) to legacy software. Opcode 1 carries flag-based actions that need no AD, one bit per action: up to 13 flags in Format B alone, up to 20 in Format C, and more by adding Format D entries. Opcode 2 is a no-operation that MUST be skipped, and opcode 127 is an extension opcode; a node that does not support it MUST drop the packet whatever the U bit says.

There is a catch with data. The top 20 bits of an LSE are often used by routers for ECMP load balancing, so changing them could reorder packets within a flow. Data that can change in transit or differ between packets of one flow MUST NOT go in those bits. That leaves 0 usable bits in Format A and B, 7 in Format C and 11 in Format D. Extra Format D entries or Post-Stack Data (from RFC 9789) are the suggested workarounds.
sections.eli5: Some notes are just a tick box, like 'yes, do this'. But routers also peek at part of each card to decide which road to use, so the changeable details have to go on the part they ignore.

sections.title: Placement and Node Responsibilities
sections.content:
The node that adds a NAS must place it where the relevant nodes can read it, within each node's Readable Label Depth (RLD). In a deep stack, several copies of a NAS may be needed. A NAS must never end up at the top of the stack at a node that does not support MNA. A Select NAS goes after the forwarding label and before the next forwarding label, and an I2E NAS needs only one copy at the bottom.

A transit node that exposes a NAS by popping a forwarding label MUST remove it, except at the penultimate hop. A penultimate node that pops the forwarding label MUST NOT remove the last HbH or I2E NAS, so the egress node can process it, and the egress node MUST remove any NAS it receives. When a node pushes labels or a new HbH NAS, it must keep the NAS within RLD and avoid conflicts with actions already present, and it SHOULD copy and merge existing HbH actions into the new NAS.

Encapsulating nodes also need to know the capabilities and RLD of the nodes on the path, and for Segment Routing the Maximum SID Depth (MSD) must include the MNA sub-stacks to be added. How that knowledge is learned is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The note has to sit near the top of the pile where each stop can see it. Every stop on the way follows the notes meant for it, and the very last stop throws the notes away.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC says MNA creates a new dimension in security concerns. The actions of an encapsulating node can affect any or all nodes along the path, the semantics of a network action are unbounded and may be insecure, and locally defined actions get limited oversight. Border nodes of an MPLS domain MUST be able to filter MNA packets arriving from a different administrative domain, and that capability MUST be implemented before MNA is deployed in the provider domain. AD may travel in the clear, so sensitive data MUST NOT be sent this way unless it is encrypted.

For compatibility, a NAS must not reach the top of the stack at an MNA-incapable node, where it will most likely be dropped. The TC and TTL of the Format A LSE are kept as they are because a legacy penultimate node may overwrite them. The RFC also covers combining a NAS with the Entropy Label and Flow-ID Label mechanisms. It lists optional counters, such as packets dropped or skipped due to unknown actions, for manageability.
sections.eli5: Because the notes can make routers do things, only trusted networks should be allowed to add them, and secret stuff should not be written on them.

sections.title: Defining New Actions and the IANA Registries
sections.content:
Section 10 updates RFC 9789: any document defining a new network action opcode MUST specify its Format (B, C or both), its Scope, the quantity, syntax and semantics of its Ancillary Data, its Processing procedure and its Interactions with other actions. If an action needs no AD, a flag is preferred because it uses only one bit.

IANA allocated label value 4 as the MNA bSPL, described as 'MPLS Network Actions', and created a registry group with two registries. The flags registry has bit positions 0 to 439 and the opcodes registry covers values 1 to 126 plus 127, with IETF Review, Experimental Use and Private Use ranges. The initial flags registry has no entries; the opcodes registry holds the special opcodes 0, 1, 2 and 127.
sections.eli5: Anyone who invents a new kind of note must write down what it looks like, who reads it and what to do with it, and then ask for a number in the official list.

fields.name: IHS
fields.desc: Scope of all actions in the NAS.

fields.name: NASL
fields.desc: Count of Format C and D LSEs in the NAS.

fields.name: NAL
fields.desc: Number of Format D LSEs that follow.

items.label: I2E
items.desc: Only the egress node processes the actions.

items.label: HbH
items.desc: All nodes along the path process the NAS.

items.label: Select
items.desc: Only specific nodes that bring the NAS to the top act on it.

items.label: bSPL protection
items.desc: Reserved and not to be used.

items.label: Flag-based NAIs
items.desc: Network actions without AD, one flag each.

items.label: No operation
items.desc: Does nothing and MUST be skipped.
